- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.3) over recent days, model tends to over-forecast, especially in the first 10–15 days of the 30d horizon — reduce early forecast peaks.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.4) and price is trending down, model often under-forecasts the drop — adjust downward bias by 5–10% in early forecast days.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior 5-day avg), model frequently overshoots in the next 5–7 days — apply a “cool-down” correction by reducing forecast by 2–5% for the following 3–5 days.
- If sentiment is volatile or mixed (±0.2–0.3), model tends to overfit recent noise — use a 3–5 day moving average filter to smooth out erratic forecast spikes.
- Mean reversion bias is evident when model holds price near recent highs — if sentiment is weak or neutral, reduce forecast by 1–3% per day for 5–7 days to allow reversion.
- For horizon >20 days, model often underestimates long-term upward trends — increase forecast by 1–3% per day for days 20–30 if sentiment is positive or neutral.
- If sentiment turns negative mid-horizon, model often fails to adjust — apply a “sentiment pivot” rule: if sentiment drops below -0.3 after day 10, reduce forecast by 2–4% per day for next 5 days.
